plan: Ten new items; topics checked against bank titles, avoiding the bank's over-used tone-of-statement WIC keys (diplomatic, equivocal, noncommittal, measured): faithful to/conditional WIC, tortoise alternative-cause inference, crow-park weakening evidence, solar-panel cleaning two-difference data, sea-monster maps cross-text, qanat synthesis with definition trap, Hunga Tonga 'Instead,', semicolon series, finite verb after long subject.

passages.title: A faithful restoration
passages.text: The restored theater is ______ its 1920s original: the architects reproduced the painted ceiling and gilded balconies exactly, altering only the wiring and plumbing hidden behind the walls.

passages.title: Returning the collection
passages.text: The museum's offer to return the carved masks to the community that made them was ______: it would take effect only if the community could show that it had climate-controlled storage for the masks.

passages.title: Giant tortoises
passages.text: Fossil sites on an island show that a species of giant tortoise disappeared at about the same time humans first arrived there. Some researchers have concluded that human hunting drove the tortoises to extinction. However, pollen preserved at the same sites shows that the island's climate became drier during that period and that the plants the tortoises ate declined sharply. Thus, the timing of human arrival alone ______

passages.title: Crows and a park
passages.text: Crows in one city avoid a particular park, even though it contains trees and food sources similar to those in parks the crows visit often. A researcher hypothesizes that the crows avoid the park because, years earlier, a scientist trapped and banded crows there, and the birds have come to associate the place with danger, not because of any feature of the park itself.

passages.title: Dusty panels
passages.text:
Researchers measured the output of solar panels under three cleaning schedules in the dry season and in the rainy season. Output is given as a percent of the panels' maximum possible output.
Cleaning schedule | Dry season | Rainy season
Weekly | 96 | 97
Monthly | 88 | 95
Never | 75 | 93
The researchers concluded that cleaning makes a much larger difference to output in the dry season than in the rainy season.

passages.title: Monsters at sea (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
The sea serpents and whales that decorate many medieval and Renaissance maps have often been read as warnings. On this view, mapmakers drew monsters in waters they considered dangerous or poorly known, telling sailors, in effect, to beware.
Text 2
A historian of cartography who traced many of these creatures to the natural-history books of the period argues that mapmakers usually believed such animals really lived where they drew them. The creatures, he suggests, were often a way of recording what was thought to be known about the oceans, and of showing off the mapmaker's skill, more than a way of marking danger.

passages.title: Underground canals
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A qanat is an underground channel that carries groundwater from the foot of a mountain to fields or towns.
• Water flows through a qanat by gravity alone.
• Qanats were first built in what is now Iran roughly 3,000 years ago.
• Because the water travels underground, much less of it evaporates than in an open canal.
• Builders dug a series of vertical shafts and then connected them with a gently sloping tunnel.

passages.title: An unusual eruption
passages.text: Most large volcanic eruptions cool the planet for a year or two, because the sulfur dioxide they release forms tiny particles that reflect sunlight. The 2022 eruption of the underwater volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai released relatively little sulfur dioxide. ______ it blasted an enormous amount of water vapor, a heat-trapping gas, into the upper atmosphere, leading some scientists to suggest that it might temporarily warm the planet rather than cool it.

passages.title: Three stops
passages.text: The research vessel's three stops on its Arctic voyage were Reykjavík, ______ Nuuk, Greenland; and Iqaluit, Canada.

passages.title: Mission Blue
passages.text: The oceanographer Sylvia Earle, who has led more than a hundred expeditions and spent thousands of hours underwater over her career, ______ the organization Mission Blue in 2009 to promote the creation of protected areas in the ocean.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: reproduced the painted ceiling and gilded balconies exactly
candidates.explanation: Exact reproduction of the visible features, with changes only to hidden systems, means the restoration closely follows the original: it is "faithful to" it.

A.rationale: The architects reproduced the visible features exactly, so the restoration did not depart from the original.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the restoration improves on the original; the point is how closely it matches.

D.rationale: A building cannot be indifferent, and the careful copying shows the opposite of indifference.

hints: Did the architects change the theater's appearance?
candidates.remember: The detail after the colon defines the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: it would take effect only if
candidates.explanation: The offer depends on a requirement ("only if"), so it is "conditional."

B.rationale: An offer that depends on a requirement being met can still fail to take effect, so it is not irrevocable.

C.rationale: The offer comes from the named museum.

D.rationale: Nothing in the text compares the offer with earlier ones.

hints: What does "only if" tell you about the offer?

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: shows that the drier climate was caused by human activity on the island.
choices.B: proves that the tortoises died out because their food plants declined.
choices.C: suggests that the tortoises had disappeared before humans arrived.
choices.D: does not establish that humans were responsible for the tortoises' extinction.

candidates.evidence: the island's climate became drier during that period
candidates.explanation: A second change (a drier climate and less food) happened at the same time, so the timing alone cannot single out hunting as the cause.

A.rationale: The text gives no cause for the drier climate.

B.rationale: The text raises the climate as a possibility; it does not prove it was the cause.

C.rationale: The text says the disappearance and human arrival happened at about the same time.

hints: What else happened at the same time?

strategy.explanation: Predict the logical conclusion about timing.

candidates.remember: When two causes coincide, timing alone cannot decide between them.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (weakening a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researcher's hypothesis?

choices.A: Crows avoided the park more strongly in the years just after the trapping than they do now.
choices.B: Crows that were never trapped themselves also avoid the park, apparently learning from other crows.
choices.C: Crows also avoid a second park, never used for trapping, with the same layout and plantings.
choices.D: The crows visit many other parks with the same kinds of trees and food sources as the avoided park.

candidates.evidence: not because of any feature of the park itself
candidates.explanation: If crows avoid an identical park that was never used for trapping, then something about the parks' features, not the trapping, may explain the avoidance. That directly weakens the hypothesis.

A.rationale: Avoidance that fades after the trapping fits the idea that the trapping caused it.

B.rationale: Learned avoidance of the trapping site is consistent with the hypothesis.

D.rationale: This rules out the shared trees and food as the cause, which supports the hypothesis.

hints: What alternative explanation does the hypothesis rule out?

strategy.explanation: Decide whether each finding supports or weakens the hypothesis.

candidates.remember: To weaken a causal claim, look for the effect without the proposed cause.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Without cleaning, output fell 21 points from weekly levels in the dry season but only 4 in the rainy season.
choices.B: Panels cleaned weekly produced 96% of maximum output in the dry season and 97% in the rainy season.
choices.C: Panels that were never cleaned produced the lowest output of the three schedules in both seasons.
choices.D: Weekly cleaning produced the highest output of the three schedules in the rainy season, 97% of maximum.

candidates.evidence: cleaning makes a much larger difference to output in the dry season
candidates.explanation: The conclusion compares the effect of cleaning across seasons. In the dry season, output falls from 96 to 75 (21 points) without cleaning; in the rainy season, from 97 to 93 (4 points).

B.rationale: This compares seasons for one schedule; it does not show how much cleaning changed output in each season.

C.rationale: This shows cleaning helps in both seasons but does not compare how much.

D.rationale: This is true but says nothing about the size of the difference in each season.

hints: What two differences does the conclusion compare?

strategy.explanation: Compute the effect of cleaning in each season.

candidates.remember: A claim about a 'larger difference' needs two differences, not single values.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the historian in Text 2 most likely respond to the view described in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the creatures were drawn mainly in waters that mapmakers had never explored
choices.B: By arguing that the creatures were copied from earlier maps without regard to their meaning
choices.C: By claiming that sailors of the period did not believe that sea monsters existed
choices.D: By arguing that many creatures recorded supposed knowledge of the seas rather than warning of danger

candidates.evidence: a way of recording what was thought to be known about the oceans
candidates.explanation: Text 1 reads the monsters as warnings about danger; Text 2 says they mostly recorded what was believed to live in the seas, and showed skill, "more than" marking danger.

A.rationale: Text 2 does not say where the creatures were drawn; it disputes their purpose.

B.rationale: Text 2 traces the creatures to natural-history books and says they reflected beliefs, not careless copying.

C.rationale: Text 2 is about what mapmakers believed, and it says they believed the animals were real.

hints: What purpose does each text give for the creatures?

strategy.explanation: State each text's view in a few words.

candidates.remember: Cross-text items often turn on a disagreement about purpose or cause.

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (explaining an advantage to a new audience)
candidates.stem: The student wants to explain an advantage of qanats to an audience unfamiliar with qanats. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Because the water in them travels underground, qanats lose far less of it to evaporation than open canals do.
choices.B: Qanats, underground channels carrying groundwater to fields by gravity, lose far less water to evaporation than open canals.
choices.C: Qanats, first built in what is now Iran roughly 3,000 years ago, move water through their tunnels by gravity alone.
choices.D: To build a qanat, workers dug a series of vertical shafts and then connected them with one gently sloping tunnel.

candidates.evidence: much less of it evaporates than in an open canal
candidates.explanation: The goal has two parts: an advantage (less evaporation) and an audience that does not know what a qanat is. Only B both defines a qanat and states the advantage.

A.rationale: This states the advantage but never explains what a qanat is, which an unfamiliar audience needs.

C.rationale: This gives history and a fact about flow but no advantage.

D.rationale: This describes construction, not an advantage.

hints: Does the audience know what a qanat is?

strategy.explanation: Check every part of the goal, including the audience.

candidates.remember: An unfamiliar audience needs the term explained.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The eruption did not release the usual cooling gas; in its place, it released a lot of a warming gas. "Instead" signals that substitution.

B.rationale: Releasing a lot of water vapor is not similar to releasing little sulfur dioxide.

C.rationale: Releasing little sulfur dioxide did not cause the eruption to release water vapor.

D.rationale: The water vapor is not a detail of the small sulfur dioxide release.

hints: What did the eruption release in place of the usual gas?

strategy.explanation: Predict the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: "Instead" introduces what happened in place of the expected thing.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: Each item contains a comma (city, country), so the items must be separated by semicolons, matching the semicolon already before "and Iqaluit."

A.rationale: Commas already separate each city from its country, so a comma here would make the list unclear; the series uses semicolons.

B.rationale: A colon cannot separate items in a list.

D.rationale: With no punctuation, "Iceland Nuuk" runs two items together.

hints: How are the later items in the list separated?

strategy.explanation: Match the punctuation already used in the series.

candidates.remember: When list items contain commas, separate the items with semicolons.

candidates.subskill: Finite verb after a long subject
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The oceanographer Sylvia Earle, who has led more than a hundred expeditions
candidates.explanation: The subject "The oceanographer Sylvia Earle" needs a main verb after the "who" clause closes; "founded" supplies it.

A.rationale: Without a finite verb, the sentence has a subject ("Sylvia Earle") but no main verb.

B.rationale: This participle phrase also leaves the sentence without a main verb.

C.rationale: A second "who" clause leaves the main clause without a verb.

hints: After the clause between commas, what does the subject do?

strategy.explanation: Cross out the clause between commas.

candidates.remember: Every sentence needs a main verb; a clause set off by commas does not count.
